newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free 38 hostages, still hold hundreds.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free 38 hostages, still hold hundreds.

text.p: Marxist rebels on Friday night released 38 of the roughly 380 hostages they held inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Peru, but said they would not surrender until their demands were met.

As the hostage crisis dragged into a fourth day and appeared far from being resolved, the freed men told the world of their grueling ordeal and implored Peru's government to relax its tough stance for the sake of those still inside.

At least 22 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, including two women, kept strict control over the hostages but had not physically or verbally harmed any of them, according to the testimonies.

They said the rebels, who addressed each other using numbers to hide their identities, had split the hostages up into different groups on the ground and first floors and allowed no communication between the groups.

The most pressing problem for those caught inside -- an influential roster of high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials -- was the lack of basic services, such as water and electricity, apparently cut off in an effort to wear down the rebels' resolve, the freed men said.
"Cutting off the services does not affect the MRTA, they are used to it," said Alex Kouri, mayor of Lima's neighbouring port Callao. "The only people who are affected are the hostages."

Despite the stressful conditions, the freed hostages said spirits among the captives were relatively high. They were cleaning the house daily and hanging onto every word of round-the-clock television coverage of the crisis.

The guerrillas sent a message with the released men promising that more hostages, a "significant" number, would be freed if the government allowed the rebels to speak by telephone with their comrades imprisoned in Peruvian jails.
But the guerrillas remained firm in their demand for the release of all jailed MRTA members -- which President Alberto Fujimori's government has already rejected.
The rebels had on Wednesday threatened to start killing their captives if their demands were not met, but have not repeated the threat since then.
As Peruvians prayed on Friday for the lives of the captives, Fujimori spent much of the day huddled with generals at a military barracks.

Ambassadors from Brazil, South Korea and Egypt were among the 38 men freed on Friday night, and formed part of a five-man "communication channel" between the rebels and the government. Eight ambassadors, three Peruvian cabinet ministers and 40 Japanese businessmen were among those left.
Red Cross officials said early on Friday some of the captives were suffering from diarrhoea, diabetes, ulcers and heart problems inside the cramped, stifling residence.
Citizens across this poor Andean nation clustered around radio sets and televisions in bars, shops and cafes seeking the latest word on the hostages.

Japan and the United States have both asked Peru to seek a peaceful solution to the crisis and put hostages' lives first. Tokyo sent Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda to Lima to push a cautious, go-slow approach in negotiations with the MRTA.
Fujimori assured (U.S.) President Bill Clinton he would do so, but the plans of the enigmatic Peruvian leader, better known for strong-arm tactics than diplomacy, were unclear.

Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi told reporters the government hoped for a peaceful end to the crisis, but police sources said preparations for a commando-style raid were being considered as one option.
Under international law, the ambassador's residence is considered Japanese territory so Fujimori must seek Tokyo's permission before taking any military action.
Negotiations by the Red Cross and a team of diplomats resulted in the entry of food, water and 16 portable toilets into the residence on Friday.

Inside, the hostages -- who include Peru's anti-terrorism chief and its foreign minister -- spent their fourth night sleeping on the floor in crumpled suits and sharing meagre rations under the gaze of their captors.

A man claiming to be an MRTA rebel telephoned Lima's CPN radio station to warn authorities against a raid on the residence. "We don't want any attack or any assault," the unidentified caller said. "We know we're dead anyway and there's nothing left but for us all to die together."
The siege was apparently meticulously planned and directed by MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini from outside via cellular telephone.

Video footage sent to Panamericana Television by the rebels showed a masked leader demonstrating a scale model of the compound to fellow rebels armed with automatic rifles, grenades and two-way radios.

Anxious relatives, chanting prayers and clutching white carnations and candles, held a peace vigil on Friday night outside the residence. Women and children planted their candles in the ground and scattered white flower petals in the shape of the words "Peace and Love."
Japan's Ikeda engaged in 20 hours of hectic non-stop diplomacy with the large Japanese community, the Canadian mediator and the U.S. ambassador but aides had no comment on the results.

So far, Fujimori's hard line against the rebels seemed popular with ordinary Peruvians, who are fed up with guerrilla violence. Citizens up and down the country hoisted national flags on makeshift masts or draped them from windows to show their support for the government.
